chunks.text: It was a bit boring. Thank you. It was good before. It was real dry. I was like- That was- All right. We are now live. Welcome, everyone. We are now hearing on- But yeah, interesting... we're on the copyright-- We're hearings on the Copyright Amendment Bill for the Social Services and Community Select Committee.

And first up, we have the member in charge of the bill, Karangi Carter. Welcome, Karangi. We have 15 minutes with you this afternoon. Thank you, Mr. Chair. It's wonderful to be here. Thank you to the committee and to all the submitters. It's a wonderful day to be in Parliament, and I think it is apt that I start with a joke. Now, I don't expect you to laugh, but this is my offering.

Knock, knock. Who's there? Who's there? Ka. Ka who? Oh. Now, that might not have been parody or satire, but- Mum joke? There it is. I could do a parody of myself. Hi, everyone. I love you so much. Life's so lovely. Yeah, there we go. No, that was a bit of satire parody.

That's it. Boom. There we go. So thank you for allowing me to speak on the Copyright Amendment Bill. In this hearing, I will leave enough time for the committee to ask questions, and I will provide some further information on this bill, as well as outlining the policy intent of this bill.

As a first-term MP, it's been really heartening to see how members' bills actually work and how many of them have gotten cross-party support, from many different viewpoints, because they have come from community, and they are looking at really specific issues that affect people in New Zealand. And a lot of them, a lot of members' bills, are outdated kind of laws, or are not fit for purpose in the modern society that New Zealand is. And it has been really heartening to see committee members really invested in making sure that we're making good legislation here.

So I commend everyone here, and thank you for your time, going through the submissions and really scrutinizing this bill in particular so that we can make sure that it is fit for purpose for the modern country that New Zealand is. One of the best things about Aotearoa is our stories, our stories told by our creatives and our artists. Their work entertains us, it educate us, and it prompts us to think about ourselves and the world around us.

Artists invoke thought provocation that helps us think about the world we want to live in and help shape the world around us. Satire and comedy specifically are some of the best tools our creatives have to convey important ideas that facilitate vital discussion and critical engagement, particularly in a democratic society. However, currently, as the law stands, artists who use material for purposes of comedy and satire are at risk of copyright

infringement. This can make for costly legal fees or the threat of costly legal fees, impedes expression, and can make our artists afraid of creating meaningful work. Over the last year, since this bill was pulled from the biscuit tin, very excitedly, I have talked to many artists from many fields about whether they have ever been sued or had threat of sue.

And what's interesting is, not a lot of court cases have actually been brought in New Zealand, but the amount of cease and desists has been huge. So people are in the middle of creating something, a company hears about it, and then they're given a cease and desist. And so, we've heard that story time and time and again, and that's art that is not being released to the world and is dampening the expression that artists have.

The other intent of this bill are-- So the intent of the Copyright Amendment Bill is to add provision to that Copyright Act 1994, like over 30 years old, to clarify that work being used for the purpose of parody and satire does not infringe copyright. So the other intent of this bill is to ensure New Zealand copyright laws are equipped to deal with both the changing media landscape, we can probably all agree that the internet's changed a little bit over the last 30 years, and bring our legislation into line with other countries such as Australia,

Canada, France, Spain, and Germany. Our copyright laws should reflect the changing nature of our media landscape. In the digital age, social media and the freedom of information that happens on the internet means that our copyright laws need to align with this change. There's been a variety of artists and creatives who have spoken in support of the bill, indicating that it could help their work to create without fear of legal challenges. Because currently, in New Zealand, artists can be sued for things that artists across

the world do every single day. You only need to look on platforms like Instagram and TikTok to see our creatives leading on the world stage. But what they are doing internationally, they could be sued for here at home because of archaic laws.

I want to be clear that although we have not seen many of these cases in court as of now, this is primarily because, as I said, that people are threatened with legal action, and then they are removing it and stopping that copyrighted work because they do not have the tens of thousands of dollars that they are threatened with. So generally, people are going to remove these works rather than go through to court against often big multinational media companies, which they don't have resource for.

Other considerations that have been raised in some of the previous submissions are around the risks of parody and satire being used to insult cultural practices or tikanga Māori, which would be awful, and we clearly do not want that. We've had one of our own MPs in this term have their makou kauae be appropriated.

That's a really tapu and real issue that happens all around the world. But what we can show is that this bill is aligned with Te Tiriti, given it promotes the advancement of Māori storytelling, social commentary, and will allow issues such as colonization and inequities against Māori to be addressed in artistic spheres.

It's also a chance for us to strengthen our Wai 262 in legislation and within the judicial system to test that it is also fit for purpose. We know that Māori have a satirical approach to storytelling. On the paepae, you'll always have a little chuckle.

Māori broadcasting has been underfunded, so this law would remove risk of financial pressures due to being fined for copyright, and the amendment must not permit misuse or disrespect of Māori works or taonga. Ongoing engagement through this process with Māori and iwi, we want to ensure that this amendment bill respects the rights of Māori and aligns with Te Tiriti.

There's so much more I could say. This bill has been an absolute pleasure to work on, and I do want to shout out to Gareth Hughes, who was the original owner of this Whakapapa Bill from the Green Party, and there was a similar bill brought by Simeon Brown not so long ago as well. So, thank you to all the creatives, to everybody who's gotten this bill to where it is now.

Yeah. Let's make some drafts, let's make some memes, and make sure that our laws in Aotearoa are fit for purpose. And I'm happy to take questions. Oh, thank you, Caroline. Helen. Hello. I don't know if you've had a chance to look at the submissions the last time you were here, but I was quite surprised by some of them.

And so there were a couple of things that were of concern. One that really stands in my mind was one where it was the capacity of AI to really parody something overnight. So you'd put out a piece of work, you'd ask AI to do a parody of it, and you were actually scraping all this. You were taking this intellectual property that belonged to the author and remodeling it, and you were actually protected if we did this from sharing any kind of intellectual property

rights of what you've done. Yeah. Thank you. Yeah, I have had a chance to have a look at them. It's been really good to see where some of the concerns are because they do align quite well, and we can go through and mitigate those, and those are going to be great questions for our advisors. With AI, this bill does not deal with AI. And as we know in this committee, we have gone around and round many committees actually. It's uncharted territory. But the important thing to come back to here is fair dealing, and what that means is if there

is somebody coming in, defaming, using, or taking this and making a big profit out of it, that is not considered fair dealing. And I think that is what needs to be really clear. When we go back to law, fair dealing is laid out in many, many different legislations, including this one, and so we can never override that fair dealing or defamation. All of those laws still apply here.

We did do quite a lot of discussing around whether we open this bill up to AI, but there is a lot of work being done in Parliament at the moment, and we want to keep this narrow and very clear. Yeah. Sorry. Yeah. What will happen under this bill- Mm-hmm... to address that concern of someone taking a work that has had a lot of time put into it and parodying it overnight? What will happen in terms of protecting the intellectual property?

Yeah, absolutely. We definitely want to protect the artist because that's what this bill essentially is about. So it's protecting artists. Yeah. So we want to make sure that there's that fine balance between protecting the artists that have actually created it. And this legislation doesn't give just open slather to anybody to use material. We have to be making sure, like I said, that it goes into that fair dealing and what you're talking about there, without specifics.

Yeah. Whether it's a video or a song or whatnot. Let's just take that. A book. Yeah. Yes. A book that has come out. I've just read one called "Taiwan Travelogue" Mm-hmm It's one book. Somebody takes that book, they AI it, they create a parody overnight. What happens then? So what you're saying is they create a parody, like a written parody or a- No, they create another book- Yeah... which has the same structure, has the same originality and takes the originality of the storyline, and it creates a work- A thing... a parody, and then it sells millions of copies.

Yeah. Thank you. That is a lot clearer. I'm not a lawyer. Yeah. But my understanding is that this legislation wouldn't protect that, but I really want to go dig into these with the advisors and the experts on the subject because there are case laws already around this topic.

And what it does is it really looks at are they taking away revenue from that artist? So are they actually taking that away? Are they defaming, and is it fair use? So the case that you're talking about is potentially similar to another case, though it wasn't written by AI.

And so it'll be good to just have a look at the screen. Yeah. I can think of many- Yeah... of course, things like you've got "Clueless" as the movie that's based on "Pride and Prejudice," I think, right? Yeah. Masses of this goes on with old books. Mm-hmm. But this might come- Sorry. Sorry. I was just Yeah. I really want to dig into this because what we want to do is make sure that artists feel like this is protecting them, and that there is an understanding of what that fair dealing, that defamation, and making sure that their

income and their work is actually protected and that's not being taken advantage of. I can't actually see that in the very small part that is-... changing in the bill. So that would be good to clarify. You mentioned a couple of things in your opening remarks. One is around the ability to use things like colonization as an example you used.

First question is, how is that stopped from being used already because it's not-... related to a publication of any sort? But the other one is around the fair dealing, and it feeds off what Helen's just asked. I'm sorry, I'm going really quickly. Yeah, we've got time. And so we're going to end up, are we going to end up in a situation where whether-- So your idea of a joke and my idea of a joke may be different.

Yeah. So are we going to end up in a situation where we're actually asking the courts to determine what is parody and satire, and what is just defamatory or abuse of an original piece of artwork, dramatization? Yes. So to your first point, yes. What we are seeing is just a small part of a bigger legislation, right?

So it works with the actual big beast that is the copyright legislation, and so that's where that fair dealing and other things come into it. And I know a lot of submitters have talked about defining what parody and satire actually is so that we're not leaving it, like you say, to the judgments.

There is conflicting advice around that, so that's something that I'd really like to get into as well, whether it actually does need to be defined, or whether under the fair dealing and under defamation laws, that actually those will, because they will all play together, that that will actually be enough.

And I haven't actually landed on whether we should have a definition or not. Though I know we've all probably got very different senses of humor. So again, that's something I really want to dig into with the advisors, and yeah, I'm just grateful that you've all been so into listening to our submitters and really trying to understand this legislation to make it as best it possibly can be.

All right, thank you very much for coming. Thank you. You don't want another joke? Does anyone want a joke? We'd love to. We do. We do need to move on. Okay, cool. Thank you all. Cheers. Thank you. Thank you. All right. Our next submitter is We Create Incorporated via Zoom.

Tēnā koutou katoa. Thank you for having me this afternoon. Good afternoon, and welcome. We Create is the alliance of 40 of Aotearoa's major creative industry associations, representing over 30,000 creatives, support people, and creative businesses across every creative discipline from screen to music, book publishing, media design, performing arts, and digital production.

Thank you for the opportunity to speak to our written submission. I'd like to use this time to bring three things to your attention that I think are essential context for your deliberations, and also that I hope will stay with you as members of both this committee and of Parliament beyond this bill. Firstly, the bill arrives in the middle of a technology revolution, and this changes everything in regard to what this bill can and should do. When Parliament last made a substantive change to the Copyright Act, ChatGPT didn't exist.

Neither did Sora, Midjourney, or the dozens of other generative AI tools that are now trained on the creative work of New Zealanders, trained without consent, without compensation, and without any usable legal framework for redress. In early June, Minister Brewer announced that Cabinet has invited him to report back in March next year on a possible copyright framework for generative AI in New Zealand. We welcome that, but it underlines something important, that the government itself has now acknowledged that the relationship

between copyright and AI is unresolved. This matters for the bill before you today. A parody and satire exception that is not precisely written does not just affect the question of whether someone can post a meme or make a satirical song or make a joke. It affects the terms in which AI companies, most of whom are operating at massive scale across borders and with enormous commercial interests that don't benefit New Zealand, can claim that their use of New Zealand creators' work is lawfully permitted.

We're not suggesting that this bill is an AI bill. What we are saying is that the days of drafting copyright exceptions as if only individual human users will rely on them are over. Mm. Every new exception in the Copyright Act is now a potential license for automated large-scale commercial exploitation by some of the world's most powerful companies.

We believe that the select committee should be alert to this. Secondly, the bill as drafted is not fit for purpose. Our written submission sets out WeCreate's position in detail, but I want to highlight what our member organizations, these are organizations that work with copyright in practice every day, have told us. Their support for a narrowly drawn exception, a carefully defined parody and satire exception modeled on what Australia introduced in 2006, is not something that the creative sector categorically opposes. Exceptions should not be implemented in isolation,

however, which is what this bill would do. They should be considered in line with an overall assessment of the act, including changes that support the needs of our creators. In particular, our members consistently flag that the legislative drafting must do the work that enforcement cannot. New Zealand is a low to no enforcement jurisdiction for copyright. The cost of taking a copyright infringement case to the High Court, and I've been there myself, is prohibitive for individual creators and small creative businesses.

In this environment, an imprecise exception does not produce balanced outcomes. It produces a free pass. Introducing a vague exception in a non-enforcement jurisdiction and leaving matters to a hypothetical but unlikely court case is not productive or helpful. Further, the bill does not define parody, and it doesn't define satire.

These are not minor drafting details. They're essential load-bearing elements of the exception. We know that Australian academics have criticized their equivalent position, sorry, provision for this exact omission, and US courts have been embroiled in constant disputes about the meaning of parody for decades. New Zealand has the advantage of being able to learn from all of this, and we should take it.

Critically, this bill is silent on mātauranga Māori, taonga works, and traditional cultural expression. These occupy a distinct moral and ethical space in Aotearoa, New Zealand. The recommendation in relation to mātauranga Māori that are contained in the Wai 262 report remain unimplemented, and we should not be passing a Copyright Act amendment that compounds existing inadequacies in the protection of taonga works by creating a broad, undefined exception that could be used to justify culturally harmful uses as protected commentary.

Thirdly, what this committee does next matters more than this bill. I want to be direct with you about something. This bill may or may not reach the House before the election. Whether it does or doesn't, the copyright issues that have surfaced will not go away. They will be on the agenda for the next parliament, the one after that, and every parliament in the foreseeable future because the technology disruption driving them is accelerating, not slowing.

The creative sector contributes $18.5 billion to our GDP. That's 4.3% of the total. Creative exports have grown at 9% compound annual growth since 2015, making the sector the fifth largest export earner. So this is not a small sector that's asking for special treatment. This is a major economic contributor asking for a regulatory framework that is fit for the digital economy.

The Copyright Act 1994 is 32 years old. It predates streaming, predates social media, and it definitely predates generative AI. The sector acknowledges that the government has recently announced a copyright term extension. We note that this is a free trade agreement obligation, and legislation to implement the new term has yet to be drafted.

A further announcement has been made on a shortlist of other copyright reforms. This includes my least favorite copyright term, locked up. Can I ask that the next time you hear locked up used in relation to copyright, you think about the artist who created the work- Mm... their connection to that work, and their moral and economic rights.

The list of further reforms has not been informed by recent engagement with WeCreate or our members. It's not extensive and doesn't prioritize the areas of copyright that we know need to be changed to effectively protect New Zealand's artists and creative businesses. We're asking this committee to use your report to call for a comprehensive, creator-centered review of the act.

The review needs to be undertaken with appropriate resourcing in both MBIE and the Ministry for Culture and Heritage in a reasonable timeline and with a mandate to legislate. The creative professionals and creative businesses in Aotearoa deserve copyright law that reflects the world they are actually working in. A world where their work can be scraped, stolen, synthesized, distributed at scale, and where the law should be their first line of protection, not an afterthought. Thank you.

Thank you, Rosh Paula. First question from Helen. First of all, I'd just like to say I totally accept that you are a weightless export that we totally underestimate- ... and that you're working in a time when things are changing so much in terms of what really valuable capital looks like.

It's in heads. One hundred percent. And we need to make sure we're talking about it. But I wanted to ask you a really practical question. You said you'd been through litigation and- Mm-hmm... how expensive it was in the copyright area. And we've had the discussion about cease and desist letters. Now, I've seen those really abused across the board in law, where cease and desist letters often have no foundation.

Mm-hmm. But they terrify people when you've got a big player. Can you just tell me about that aspect of it? Are we failing in litig-- in our justice system and our protection of property systems, et cetera, and our civil law system because the cease and desist letter is being abused?

In my experience, so a declaration, I spent 12 years running Copyright Licensing New Zealand, which is the licensing agency for publishing and visual artists. So I was, I think, the last person to take a case to the copyright tribunal. That's definitely not for the faint of heart, and certainly not good for the bank account. I'm interested in how people think cease and desist letters are being abused. In my experience, we used to send them as an agency that worked on behalf of authors, but the predominant other party that we were sending them to were the digital platforms.

Mm-hmm. They weren't other New Zealanders or New Zealand media businesses here, but they weren't local. And our challenge was to actually get any sort of useful response from those platforms was next to impossible. The last thing I had underway prior to leaving copyright licensing, was a case where there'd been 120 New Zealand Maori writers' books digitized and made available for sale on Facebook. Now, trying to get any form of appropriate removal of that work or any sort of action out of Facebook

was-- I spent months on it and got nowhere. So completely accept that there are a need for meaningful enforcement mechanisms that also have the flip side of them, which is that we're not providing a mechanism for things to be sent in circumstances where there's no legal basis.

Thank you. Great beginning of a discussion. Yeah. Thanks. Thanks, Paula. Can I just-- sorry, we're out of time, but just to distill my understanding of your submission. Is it that you-- this is surfacing an important issue, but this bill isn't addressing enough of the issues at this point in your submission?

No. The copyright exceptions, whether they are applied to fair dealing or however they sit within the legislation, obviously we don't have fair use here. It's clearly fair dealing, which is a permission-based, legislative-based framework rather than a sue me framework. That's why you need the wider consideration of the whole of the act together, because where you're making adjustments will have impacts on other parts of the legislation.

Mm. And you often see exceptions used in combination with each other, not in isolation. So it's very difficult to make a-- The one thing that would be easy to make to the act would be a term extension change because you're literally changing some numbers in the legislation. But when you're looking at exceptions, no, it's way more complicated, and just trying to do one and think that you're done, it needs to sit in a broader review.

Great. Thank you very much for your submission this afternoon. Appreciate it. Thank you for hearing me. Thanks, Paula. Thank you. Kia ora. All right, our next submitter is Nicholas Birling. He's via Zoom. Via Zoom as well. Okay, excellent.

Good afternoon, Nicholas. Welcome to the Social Services and Community Select Committee. We've got five minutes with you this afternoon. The time is yours when you're ready. Thank you for hearing me, members of the select committee. Just a quick personal background.

I wrote my master's thesis on this particular area, so I'm really an interested member of the public, even though, of course, I am a lawyer, as I say in my submission. Just picking up on some of the things that have been said that relate to my submission. I used to think that definitions would be a problem, and in fact, my thesis says that you can get hung up on satire and parody. And the Americans have had a lot of trouble with it, as Paula Browning, the submitter before me, said. And they've got into a lot of paper and a lot of

discussion about where one ends and where the other begins. I've changed my view to some extent because the Australians do not seem to have had a problem with definitions. And I've got a decision in front of me. It's called AGL Energy Limited against Greenpeace.

I referred to it in my submission. Justice Birley, no relation to me, says in that case, that the problem with definitions is, and I'm taking a bit of liberty with what he says, is perhaps more of an apparent problem than a real one. So, it seems to me as though the definitions themselves are probably not going to be a problem on the Australian experience.

In terms of the fair dealing defense, and this is something that relates to Helen White, what Helen White said before, and AI and potential abuse Any defense here would have to fit within the fair dealing exception. And again, I'm looking at another case.

Oh, have I disappeared? No, we still got you. We can hear you. Yeah. There are a list of things that the law has said you look at. So there's the purpose and character of the dealing, the nature of the work or the adaptation, the possibility of getting or obtaining the work within a reasonable time at an ordinary commercial cost, effects of the dealing on the potential market.

So, those factors are a safeguard to stop what I might call a free-for-all. So in general, I say in my submission, the amendment is not perfect, but it's a good start, and plenty of other jurisdictions, whether they're common law ones or not, have this type of exception, often for just parody rather than satire.

But certainly, some jurisdictions have both. I'm happy to answer questions. I'm just noting the time. No. Thank you, Nicholas. Any questions, members? Okay. You are coming from a different position from quite a few of the submitters, and so it would be nice to know what you think about the AI example.

Well, with the AI example, I must confess, I am not particularly competent in that area. But it seems to me that some of the fear can be balanced out, at least to some extent, by the fair dealing defense and what you actually have to show if you're trying to rely on this defense.

Because it is, after all, the person who infringes copyright who has to justify it. So, if you go through those factors, and because it's common law, there are a number of factors. The factors I've read out are just some. There are others, depending on the case. If you go through them, a balancing then can be created.

I've got another case here. It's another Australian one, where a politician used a well-known song for election purposes or political purposes. Oh, yeah . And there was simply no way that was considered to be fair dealing. Mm. Yeah. Okay. But now, in terms of the AI, I'm sorry, I don't know of a case.

I can't specifically answer your question with a case. Thank you very much. Can I ask about the trademarks? I think we're stretching our time. We need to finish at 1:00 . Okay. All right. But- Thank you very much... thank you. Okay. Thank you. Appreciate you making a submission this afternoon. Yeah. Thank you very much. Thank you.

Right, our next submitter is, we have actually one who's been able to make it, so we're moving to Ms. Debbie Port, in person. Welcome. I'm glad you guys were talking about AI, because I actually use it to create my content. Anyway I think a lot of people are using it these days. Make loads of money out of people like Winston Peters, but anyway.

Right. Welcome. And I've got content on there if you guys want to see it. Now, I understand it from both sides, because last year, I had to serve a cease and desist notice on somebody for using a photo of mine without my consent. And so I asked Google what to do. So I did that, I put it on their door, and then I told the landlord, because this is another tenant.

And under RTI, there's stuff to do with this, and the landlord made sure that tenant removed the content that they had illegally used without my consent or knowledge. So I understand that side of it. Because this person tried to take credit for my work and tried to say they owned the photo, when, no, that's not true. And that was successful. So yeah. But now I create my own content, and it's a form of therapy for me.

Somebody suggested I do art therapy, and this is a form of therapy for me because of what I've been through. And so I create. I've got an AI thing of Winston Peters on a broomstick and falling off and going, "Bloody workers, get out of my way." And I actually posted that to YouTube in my submission for you guys to look at. That's actually AI.

If you want to go and have a look at that link, it's there for people to watch. There we go . She's got it. Yeah . I'm sorry. My apologies. Sorry. We're timely, but we play at the same time. And it had the Jaws theme song in it. And it was only meant to be a short version of that song, not the whole...

Yeah. Anyway. Yeah. So, I had added that as a point of copyright, right? And I'm not making money off what I'm doing. And I've got other videos. Winston Peters on there as well, if you want to have a look at the other videos. I was playing it outside ACTE year. So that's what I do. And I don't want to be prosecuted for having a sense of humor, thank you. I grew up when we had all that parody stuff on TV, and Dolly did it, and yeah, Comedy Company over in Australia. Yeah. So, mm.

Excellent. Billy T. James . Yeah. Any questions? Any questions, members? I do have a question. Yeah. Go, Carrie. I've heard a lot of people make memes, even if they're just for their own consumption- Yeah... as a form of therapy or- Yeah... to sort of deal with what they do. Do you make memes?

No, I do videos. You do videos. So what I do is I picture first ChatGPT and MusicGPT, right? So, it's the photo and the lyrics, and I always put political satire in it, because it won't do stuff otherwise. ChatGPT is very restrictive, right? And you put that in, get the content, and then I go to a website to put it all together into a video form so I can upload it to Facebook.

And I've posted quite a few on Tamison Falls Facebook page. I'm interested- He's actually a friend of mine, so yeah. So I actually posted it to... And also Gerard Otto, I posted it to his Facebook page, and Winston Peters' Facebook page, I put my content about him on there. I created a picture of him in a cave in 1550, playing with a Bunsen burner and a broomstick on the side. Yeah, so I've created several So none of us are safe from your- No... potential videos.

No, he's pretty easy. He was having a go about flags flying at Parliament a while back. Hmm. And the word nob waffle came up. So I created a nob waffle anthem and, yeah. So pretty easy So what did you use to express your creativity before ChatGPT and MusicGPT? Oh, I used to write stuff down, create poetry and stuff.

Oh, yeah. Yeah, so I've been doing this for years. But the humorous stuff, yeah, it's just my way of coping- Yeah... when something happens. It's like, let's just forget the world and just poke fun at it. Yeah. Yeah, yeah. So you're finding these tools are able to sort of help you express your creativity more fully? Yeah. Like my mother's death. Yeah. Yeah.

I'm sorry to hear that. Sorry to hear that. It's all right. We've all got to go sometime, but you know what. Yeah, yeah. You're quite right. She didn't need to hear that. Now don't you punish me. Any more questions? Thank you very much. Yeah. No, look, thank you very much, and thank you for your fabulous submission- Not a problem... so far. I appreciate it.

So yeah, so I've uploaded a few videos there. And I'll upload a few more- ... so you can be entertained. Thank you. Oh, good on you. Lovely to meet you. You as same here. Cool. Thanks. See you. Have a good day. Right. This next matter online is Professor Tony Bayston. Or Troy, sorry. Troy. My mistake.

Very good. Thank you. Thank you very much. Yes, I would've corrected you, but I wasn't getting my-... audio on fast enough. No. But yes, thanks for hearing this. Let me just get my cursor back on my submission. Look, I'll just take you through a few points very quickly. One of the first ones is I am an expert in many things, but I'm not an expert in the law around this. But what I will say is, compared to comparable democracies, I'm obviously from the US, have been working in and through New Zealand for 25 years, it does feel like something's missing

here in terms of our ability to succeed in getting complex ideas across, and the complex issues that our society faces sorted out. And so one of the things I think that can help with that is parody and satire. I have nothing to say about the complex legal issues that you have to sort through, but what I do think is that this works on both sides of the political spectrum, whether it's activists or corporations, government with huge piles of corporate comms staff.

Parody and satire are a great way to start to make progress getting through a complex issue so that there's actually buy-in and engagement with it. You sort of saw that from the last speaker. She really gets off doing that and is willing to turn up to engage in ideas because she's able to do it in a way that's funny.
